opus-5.5.text:
Honestly, I wouldn't call it a grand belief at the start. It was more a gut feeling that something didn't add up. At the time, almost every diffusion model used a U-Net backbone. That was just the default everyone inherited, and very few people asked whether it was actually necessary. Meanwhile, transformers were taking over language and much of vision recognition, and they had this very clean scaling behavior: add compute, add parameters, and things get predictably better.

So the question in my head was simple. Is the U-Net's inductive bias really essential for generation, or is it historical baggage? If it's baggage, then replacing it with a plain transformer could let image generation ride the same scaling curve as everything else. That felt like a question worth answering either way. Even a negative result would have taught us something.

As for skepticism, I think it's natural. People ask, "U-Net works, why change it?" or "Transformers are expensive on images, isn't this wasteful?" Those are reasonable concerns. But I've always felt research shouldn't just be incremental tuning on a structure everyone already accepts. The most valuable work often challenges a default people stopped questioning.

There's also a personal side. I like simple, general designs. The idea of unifying architectures, the same kind of model for understanding and for generation, was aesthetically very appealing to me. When something is both simple and scalable, I tend to trust it will matter eventually, even if the immediate payoff isn't obvious.

And Bill Peebles, who drove the project, was very determined, so we kept going. Looking back, what made it convincing wasn't any single number. It was seeing a clear trend: as we scaled the model, quality improved steadily. Once you see that kind of curve, you know you're onto something real.

r001.rationale: The response describes DiT as a worthwhile question and an appealing, potentially scalable alternative, but does not say Xie viewed it as an unavoidable direction for diffusion-model architecture.

fable-5.1.text:
Honestly, "believe" might be too strong a word for how it felt at the time. It was more like a stubborn hunch. When Bill Peebles and I started working on DiT, the prevailing view was that the U-Net was just the right architecture for diffusion. It had all these inductive biases built in, the convolutions, the skip connections, the multi-scale structure, and people thought those were essential to making diffusion work. So replacing it with a plain transformer looked, to a lot of people, like a step backwards. Why throw away all that structure for something that's supposedly less sample-efficient?

But I had been living with transformers in vision for a while, and I had watched the same story play out before. With ViT, with ConvNeXt, every time people said a domain needed special architectural inductive biases, it turned out that given enough data and enough compute, the simpler, more general architecture caught up and then surpassed. The inductive bias was helping at small scale and hurting at large scale. So my intuition was that diffusion would not be the exception. It was just one more generative modeling problem, and there was no deep reason it should require a U-Net.

The other thing that mattered a lot to me was scalability as a research question in itself. With the U-Net, there wasn't really a clean way to ask, if I give you ten times the compute, how much better do you get? The architecture was a bit of a mess for that. Transformers give you a very clean knob. You have depth, width, number of tokens, and you can plot FID against Gflops and actually see a line. When we first saw that curve, that was the moment it went from a hunch to something I was willing to defend in a meeting. The scaling behavior was so clean that it felt like we had found the right abstraction, regardless of whether the numbers at that moment were state of the art.

And I'll admit that the opposition was not unreasonable. Our first results were not better than the best U-Nets. If you only looked at the headline number, you could easily say this doesn't work. So the argument I had to make internally was not "we beat everything," it was "look at the slope, not the point." That's a harder sell, because you're asking people to bet on a trend rather than a result. But I had been through that argument enough times in my career that I was comfortable being the person in the room who sounded a little naive.

The last piece is just taste, I think. I like simple things. I like when you can explain an architecture in one sentence and there's nothing clever hiding in it. DiT is very boring in that sense, which I consider a compliment. And boring things tend to be the ones that survive, because everyone can build on them. So even in the version of the world where DiT turned out to be only comparable rather than better, I thought the simplicity alone made it worth pursuing. That it ended up becoming the backbone for Sora and a lot of video and image models afterwards was, frankly, more than I expected at the time.

r001.rationale: The response says X expected transformers to scale well in diffusion and saw no deep reason diffusion required a U-Net, but it does not state that DiT was an unavoidable direction for architecture evolution.

astra-6.text:
For me, the core question was simple: if transformers could scale so effectively in other domains, could they also be a strong backbone for diffusion models? At the time, U-Nets were the standard, and they worked very well. So it was reasonable for people to ask why we should replace them.

But I felt that the question was worth testing. We weren’t just trying to make a different architecture; we wanted to understand whether there was a simpler, more scalable foundation for generative modeling. Even if the initial results weren’t better, that wouldn’t necessarily settle the question. We needed to see how the approach behaved as we increased compute and model size.

That was the motivation for pursuing it: there was a clear hypothesis, and experiments could tell us whether it was right. You don’t need everyone to agree before you run those experiments.

r001.rationale: The response says DiT was worth testing as a potentially simpler, more scalable foundation, but does not describe it as an unavoidable direction for diffusion-model architecture.

sol-6.1.text:
For me, the core question was whether we could make diffusion models benefit from the same kind of scalable architecture that was working so well in other areas. Transformers were a natural candidate, but it wasn’t obvious that replacing the U-Net would work, or that it would be worth the effort.

I thought that uncertainty was a reason to run the experiment. If we could keep the diffusion framework and change the backbone, we could ask a fairly clean question: how does that architectural choice affect performance as we scale compute?

So my conviction wasn’t that DiT was guaranteed to succeed. It was that the question was important enough to test, and that even a negative result would teach us something useful.

r001.rationale: The candidate says DiT was an important question to test, but describes it as uncertain and does not say it was an unavoidable direction for diffusion-model architecture.
